title: 3-Read Friday #99: Teacher Cognitive Load, Testing Reform, and Ratio Tables
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #99 opens with Joel Kenyon applying cognitive load theory to teachers themselves, arguing schools must stop overloading staff with performative administrative tasks that crowd out the mental bandwidth genuine teaching requires. Natalie Wexler then tells the story of Louisiana's discontinued Innovative Assessment pilot, showing that testing students on actual curriculum content rather than decontextualised skills pushed teachers toward knowledge-building instruction and narrowed achievement gaps -- before the experiment was ended too early for deeper change to take hold. Jon Fant closes with a maths-specific piece arguing that ratio tables give students a unified proportional framework for deriving area and volume conversion factors by squaring and cubing linear relationships, replacing fragmented memorisation with structural understanding. Barton's throughline connects teacher workload, assessment design, and mathematical structure as three different fronts in the same fight against fragmentation and overload.
points: Cognitive load theory isn't just a student-facing framework -- Kenyon's argument is that performative admin overloads teachers' own working memory, directly degrading the teaching they can deliver.

Louisiana's Innovative Assessment pilot is a natural experiment showing curriculum-aligned testing shifts teacher behaviour toward knowledge-building and narrows gaps, but Wexler's account is also a cautionary tale about reform being cut short before it compounds.

Fant's ratio-table approach replaces fragmented, formula-by-formula memorisation of area/volume conversions with one structural idea -- squaring and cubing a linear ratio -- that generalises across contexts.
Across the three picks, the shared lesson is that fragmentation -- of teacher time, of assessment design, of mathematical procedure -- is the recurring obstacle to durable improvement.
